name: Armbar from closed guard

primary_target.mechanism: Elbow hyperextension: the attacker's hips act as the fulcrum below the elbow while the wrist is pulled to the chest; forearm kept neutral/thumb-up so the olecranon locks in the fossa and the medial elbow complex (UCL, flexor origin, anterior capsule) is loaded in tension
primary_target.plain: Your hips act as a lever under their elbow while you pull the wrist to your chest, bending the elbow the wrong way (hyperextension). With their thumb pointing up, the tip of the elbow locks out and the ligaments, tendons and joint lining on the inside and front of the elbow are stretched.

secondary_targets.mechanism: Arm is pulled across and up; knees pinch the upper arm, limiting rotation
secondary_targets.plain: The arm is pulled across and up while your knees pinch the upper arm, so the shoulder cannot turn to escape.

positions.note: Break posture, control the wrist/sleeve, angle the hips, leg over the head, squeeze knees and lift hips
Same finish from open guard once an arm is isolated

ibjjf.note: Not on the IBJJF prohibited-techniques table (Rules Book v6.1 p. 29); legal in every division including kids

summary: The classic cross armlock from the guard: pull the arm across your centreline, swing a leg over the head, pinch the knees and raise the hips to hyperextend the elbow.
notes: Which structure fails first is debated: the 2017 MRI case series found UCL and common flexor tendon injury; a cadaver study reported second-hand (Sherdog) found anterior capsule rupture first.

name: Armbar from mount / S-mount / technical mount

primary_target.mechanism: Elbow hyperextension over the attacker's hips/pelvis with the wrist pinned to the chest and the forearm neutral; knees squeezed to immobilise the humerus
primary_target.plain: Their wrist is pinned to your chest and the elbow is bent the wrong way over your hips (hyperextension), with their thumb pointing up; your knees squeeze the upper arm so it cannot move. This stretches the ligaments and tendons on the inside and front of the elbow.

positions.note: Isolate one arm (often when the opponent pushes the chest), step to S-mount, swing the leg over the head and sit back
The S-mount pins the arm against the attacker's thigh and blocks the head with the knee before the finish
Technical mount gives direct access to the far/top arm for the armbar
Near-arm armbar when the opponent pushes the knee

summary: From mount the attacker climbs to S-mount, traps the arm against the thigh, swings the leg over the head and sits back for the hyperextension.

name: Armbar from side control (far-arm / spinning armbar)

primary_target.mechanism: Elbow hyperextension: the far arm is isolated under the attacker's armpit or across the chest, the attacker steps/spins over the head and extends the elbow over the hips or the thigh
primary_target.plain: The far arm is trapped under your armpit or across your chest, then you step over the head and straighten the elbow past its limit over your hips or thigh (hyperextension), stretching the joint and ligaments on the inside and front of the elbow.

positions.note: Trap the far arm (e.g., when the opponent pushes on the hip/face), step over the head and spin to the armbar; Theory & Technique lists 'Arm bar from across-side position'
Arm isolated while circling to north-south
Spinning armbar on the far arm

summary: Top-side armlock: isolate the far arm, step over the head and fall back into the cross armlock.

sources.locator: entry 'Arm bar from across-side position' (LibraryThing contents listing)

name: Armbar from back control

primary_target.mechanism: Elbow hyperextension: from the back the attacker traps the arm (often with a kimura or wrist grip), swings a leg over the head and falls to the side to extend the elbow over the hips
primary_target.plain: From the back you trap the arm, swing a leg over the head and fall to the side, bending the elbow the wrong way over your hips (hyperextension) and stretching the joint and ligaments on the inside and front of the elbow.

positions.note: When the opponent defends the choke with the hands, trap the top arm and rotate to the armbar; Kesting lists armbars from 'kimura control from the back'
See armbar_crucifix

summary: A choke-defence counter from the back: control the arm, throw the leg over the head and extend the elbow.
notes: Garcia 2011 covers finishing from the back but exact pages were not verified.

name: Armbar from spider guard

primary_target.mechanism: Elbow hyperextension: the sleeve grip pulls the arm while the foot on the biceps pushes the upper arm, pre-extending the elbow; the attacker angles the hips and throws the leg over the head to finish
primary_target.plain: The sleeve grip pulls the arm while your foot on their biceps pushes it, so the elbow is already straight; you angle your hips and swing the leg over the head to bend the elbow the wrong way (hyperextension), stretching the joint and ligaments on the inside and front of the elbow.

positions.note: Pull the sleeve, push the biceps with the foot, move the other foot to the hip, swing the leg over the head (gi)
Lasso isolates the arm for the same finish

ibjjf.note: Spider/lasso grips require the gi sleeve; no-gi equivalents use wrist control

summary: Gi-specific armbar: the sleeve-and-foot-on-biceps tension already straightens the arm, so the attacker only has to angle and swing the leg over the head.

name: Flying armbar

primary_target.mechanism: Elbow hyperextension: from standing the attacker controls the arm (and collar/neck in no-gi), places a shin on the opponent's hip/midsection, jumps and swings the other leg over the head, landing in the cross armlock
primary_target.plain: You jump from standing into the same armbar: the arm ends up across your hips and the elbow is bent the wrong way (hyperextension), stretching the joint and ligaments on the inside and front of the elbow.

positions.note: Usually against a collar tie or a stiff arm; high risk if the opponent does not support the weight

ibjjf.note: The armbar itself is legal, but IBJJF Rules Book v6.1 item 6.2.2 W penalises jumping to closed guard 'including any and all attacks initiated by jumping guard, such as ... Flying Triangles and Flying Armbars' in all under-15 divisions and all white-belt age groups

summary: A standing jump into the cross armlock; spectacular but risky, and effectively banned for white belts and under-15s under IBJJF rules.

name: Armbar from the crucifix (leg-trapped arm)

primary_target.mechanism: Elbow hyperextension using the legs: the arm trapped between the attacker's thighs is straightened and the attacker bridges the hips forward against the elbow while the legs are triangled to remove slack
primary_target.plain: The arm trapped between your thighs is straightened and you push your hips forward against the elbow, bending it the wrong way (hyperextension) with your legs instead of your hands, stretching the joint and ligaments on the inside and front of the elbow.

positions.note: Bottom-leg triangle version, or top-leg triangle after the opponent turns the arm (hitchhiker)

summary: With one arm captured between the legs in the crucifix, the attacker extends the elbow with a hip bridge instead of the hands.

name: Helicopter armbar

primary_target.mechanism: Elbow hyperextension: the attacker grips both arms, falls backward with feet on the hips (tomoe-nage), lifts and rotates the opponent over, and lands with the extended arm across the hips
primary_target.plain: After the sacrifice throw you land with their straight arm across your hips, so the elbow is bent the wrong way (hyperextension), stretching the joint and ligaments on the inside and front of the elbow.

positions.note: Entered from a double-arm grip or double sleeve grip while standing

ibjjf.note: Not a jumping-guard entry, so not covered by 6.2.2 W; slamming the opponent on landing would be a slam (prohibited at all levels)

summary: A sacrifice-throw armbar: sit back under the opponent with feet on their hips, spin them over and come up in the armlock.
notes: Only a Wikipedia description was located; no textbook locator.

name: Reverse armbar from closed guard

primary_target.mechanism: Elbow hyperextension with the arm clamped across the attacker's chest/shoulder: the elbow is rolled to point up (shoulder internally rotated, thumb down), the attacker's shoulder or forearm acts as the fulcrum under the elbow, and the hands/chest pull the wrist down so the joint 'cuts' over the fulcrum
primary_target.plain: Their arm is clamped across your chest with the elbow turned to point up (thumb down); your shoulder or forearm sits under the elbow as the pivot while you pull the wrist down, bending the elbow the wrong way (hyperextension) and stretching the joint and ligaments on the inside and front of the elbow.

secondary_targets.mechanism: Shoulder line is controlled and internally rotated to expose the elbow
secondary_targets.plain: Their shoulder is held and rolled inward (thumb down) so the elbow points up and is exposed.

positions.note: Overhook/clamp the arm to your chest, roll the elbow up and 'cut' with the shoulder; doubles as a sweep set-up
Same finish from butterfly guard (Biernacki)
Hage shows entries from half guard

summary: Instead of a leg over the head, the elbow is straightened against your own shoulder or forearm with the arm trapped across your chest.
notes: Judo names vary: ude-gatame (arm lock with hands) / waki-gatame (armpit) are near equivalents.

name: Reverse / straight armbar from side control and passing

primary_target.mechanism: Elbow hyperextension against a fulcrum formed by the attacker's shoulder, neck or forearm: the opponent's wrist is trapped (under the armpit or on the shoulder) and the elbow is lifted/pressed with the elbow tightly controlled so it cannot rotate out
primary_target.plain: Their wrist is trapped under your armpit or on your shoulder and the elbow is pressed over your shoulder, neck or forearm as the pivot, bending it the wrong way (hyperextension); holding the elbow tight stops them turning out of it. This stretches the joint and ligaments on the inside and front of the elbow.

positions.note: Against a stiff frame or the near arm pushing on the hip; works in combination with the figure-four (americana/kimura) grips
Against the frame/underhook attempt while passing
When the opponent pushes the knee with a straight arm

summary: A top-position straight armlock on a framing arm: pin the wrist, control the elbow tightly and press the joint over your shoulder/forearm.
notes: No textbook locator found for the side-control version.

name: Kimura

structures: posterior band of the inferior glenohumeral ligament / posterior capsule
primary_target.mechanism: Forced internal (medial) rotation plus extension of the humerus with the elbow flexed ~90 deg, driving the hand up behind the back; a figure-four grip (one hand on the wrist, the other through and gripping your own wrist) uses the forearm as a lever
primary_target.plain: With the elbow bent at a right angle, the figure-four grip uses their forearm as a lever to drive the hand up behind their back, twisting the shoulder joint inward and backward. This stretches the back of the shoulder joint and the rotator cuff, and can strain the joint on top of the shoulder where the collarbone meets the shoulder blade.

secondary_targets.mechanism: If the elbow is allowed to open, torque is transmitted to the elbow (double wristlock origin)
secondary_targets.plain: If they let the elbow straighten, the twist moves into the elbow and strains the ligaments on its inside.

secondary_targets.mechanism: The wrist grip can bend the wrist as a finishing adjunct
secondary_targets.plain: The hand on their wrist can also bend the wrist as an extra finish.

positions.note: Far-arm kimura; most commonly taught; circle to north-south to finish
Kesting: strongest finishing position; opponent turned on side, arm driven behind the back in a triangle-shaped motion
Sit up, trap the posting arm with the figure-four, fall to the side and swing the arm behind the back; doubles as a sweep
Attack the far arm when the opponent frames on your face or reaches for the back
Kimura grip from half guard bottom feeds sweeps, back takes and the finish
Topside kimura control vs turtle; roll the opponent over to finish
Kimura control from the back (especially no-gi)
When the opponent turns or frames
Standing kimuras; classic counter to a single-leg takedown (kimura grip on the attacker's wrist)

ibjjf.note: Not on the prohibited table; legal in all divisions

summary: Figure-four bent-arm shoulder lock that rotates the arm inward and up behind the back; Masahiko Kimura used it to beat Helio Gracie in 1951.

sources.locator: posterior-band IGHL elongation at 90 deg abduction + internal rotation

notes: Anatomical loading: internal rotation tensions the posterior capsule/posterior IGHL and the external rotators; the frequently quoted 'subscapularis' target is actually the muscle being shortened, not stretched.

name: Americana

structures: anterior band of the inferior glenohumeral ligament
primary_target.mechanism: Forced external rotation of the humerus with the shoulder abducted ~90 deg and the elbow flexed ~90 deg: the wrist is pinned to the mat and the elbow is lifted/dragged toward the hip ('paintbrush'), loading the anterior capsule and anterior IGHL - the apprehension position
primary_target.plain: With the arm out to the side and the elbow bent at a right angle, you pin the wrist to the mat and lift or slide the elbow toward their hip (the 'paintbrush'), twisting the shoulder joint backwards (palm-up direction). This stretches the ligaments and joint lining at the front of the shoulder - the position where shoulders dislocate forward.

secondary_targets.mechanism: Elbow is flexed and used as the lever; some torque reaches the elbow if the wrist slides
secondary_targets.plain: The bent elbow is the lever; if the wrist slides, some of the twist goes into the elbow.

positions.note: Near-arm keylock when the opponent pushes with the far hand or frames; pin wrist, thread the other hand under the elbow, grip your own wrist
Drive the wrist to the mat with body weight, then lift the elbow
Far-arm americana while passing
Americana/keylock on the hand-controlled arm

ibjjf.note: Not on the IBJJF prohibited table; legal in every division. (Some other federations restrict it for children - not IBJJF.)

summary: Figure-four lock where the forearm points up: pin the wrist, lift the elbow and rotate the shoulder outward.

sources.locator: anterior-band IGHL max elongation at 90 deg abduction + max external rotation

notes: Name origin (Rolls Gracie / Bob Anderson) is disputed; the term appears in a 1951 Brazilian newspaper.

name: Omoplata

structures: posterior capsule / posterior band of the inferior glenohumeral ligament
primary_target.mechanism: Forced internal rotation (and extension) of the humerus using the leg: the attacker's hamstring/leg is clamped over the back of the shoulder with the forearm trapped behind it, the attacker sits up and drives forward and down so the hand is pushed up the back
primary_target.plain: Your leg wraps over the back of their shoulder with their forearm trapped behind it; you sit up and lean forward and down so their hand is pushed up their back, twisting the shoulder joint inward and backward. This stretches the back of the shoulder joint and the rotator cuff.

secondary_targets.mechanism: Elbow is bent and trapped; pressure may reach it if the arm is straightened
secondary_targets.plain: The elbow is bent and trapped; it can take pressure if the arm is straightened.

positions.note: Classic entry when the opponent posts/grips; break posture, bring the leg over the shoulder, pivot 90-180 deg, sit up, control the hip/belt to stop the forward roll
Foot-on-biceps leg swings over the shoulder (gi)
The lasso converts directly into the omoplata by swinging the free leg over
Bravo's rubber guard flowchart lists the omoplata from Mission Control / New York
Mounted omoplata/step-over on a trapped arm

ibjjf.note: Prohibited in the 4-12 and 13-15 age divisions (IBJJF table row 6); legal from 16 years, all belts

summary: A kimura done with the leg: the leg wraps over the shoulder, trapping the arm behind the back, and the attacker sits up and leans forward.
notes: Kids' prohibition verified against the rendered table on 2026-10-11.

name: Baratoplata

primary_target.mechanism: Forced internal rotation: the opponent's elbow is clamped between the attacker's thighs (triangle-like), the attacker threads an arm through the bent arm (reverse-kimura frame seated in the elbow crook) and pushes the wrist outward and upward while turning the torso toward the trapped shoulder
primary_target.plain: Their elbow is clamped between your thighs and your arm is threaded through the bend of their elbow; you push their wrist out and up while turning your body toward the trapped shoulder, twisting the shoulder joint inward. This stretches the back of the shoulder joint and the rotator cuff.

positions.note: Reverse-kimura grip, wrist pinned to the belly, elbow trapped by the thighs, angle the hips
From a defended mounted armbar: thread the arm through the elbow and lock the figure-four
Against an extended frame, step over the head
From armbar/triangle control

ibjjf.note: A shoulder lock, not on the prohibited table; Caio Terra won the 2015 IBJJF No-Gi Worlds final with it

summary: Rafael 'Barata' Freitas' shoulder lock: elbow pinned between the thighs, your arm threaded through the crook, wrist pushed out and up.
notes: Sources disagree on the precise direction of the finishing torque (rotate torso vs push arm away); Freitas originally developed it as a bicep slicer and converted it to a shoulder lock for rules compliance.

name: Tarikoplata

primary_target.mechanism: Forced internal rotation: starting from a kimura (figure-four) grip, the attacker swings a leg over the opponent's shoulder line so the shin/calf becomes the frame, transfers the grip to the own thigh/shin and rotates the captured arm toward the attacker's head with hip and leg torque
primary_target.plain: From a kimura grip you swing a leg over their shoulder so your shin or calf becomes the frame, move your grip to your own leg and use your hips and leg to rotate their arm toward your head, twisting the shoulder joint inward. This stretches the back of the shoulder joint and the rotator cuff.

positions.note: Knee-shield/Z-guard with underhook to isolate the arm, then swing the leg over
From a stalled kimura or omoplata
When the kimura is defended by gripping the belt/gi, step the leg over the head/shoulder
Same transition from a defended kimura/armbar

ibjjf.note: Shoulder lock, not on the prohibited table

summary: Tarik Hopstock's kimura finished with a leg over the shoulder for extra leverage; the elbow is pulled inward toward your core (opposite of the baratoplata's push).

name: Monoplata

primary_target.mechanism: Forced internal rotation/hyper-rotation with the arm trapped: one leg drapes over the opponent's back and hooks the arm near the elbow (arm held above the hips and under the armpit), the attacker's thigh and ribs control the arm and hip pressure drives into the shoulder
primary_target.plain: One leg drapes over their back and hooks the arm near the elbow; your thigh and ribs hold the arm and your hips drive into the shoulder, twisting the shoulder joint inward past its limit. This stretches the back of the shoulder joint and the rotator cuff.

positions.note: From 3/4 mount when the opponent turns to take an underhook; separate the arm, lean and swing the leg to trap it
Reaction to the underhook pummel
From triangle control when the opponent hides the arm; hip-bump into the monoplata

ibjjf.note: Shoulder lock, not on the prohibited table

summary: An omoplata-style shoulder lock applied with one leg from on top (3/4 mount), popularised by Marcelo Garcia; converts to an armbar if the arm straightens.
notes: Sources differ on which leg traps the arm; terminology also varies (some schools call a reverse omoplata 'monoplata').

name: Marceloplata

primary_target.mechanism: Forced internal rotation of the trapped arm, as in the omoplata, re-secured when the opponent is slipping out of the standard finish (the arm is re-clamped and the shoulder re-torqued from a modified leg/hip configuration)
primary_target.plain: The same inward twist of the shoulder as the omoplata: when they are slipping out, you re-clamp the arm with a changed leg and hip position and twist the shoulder again. This stretches the back of the shoulder joint and the rotator cuff.

positions.note: Follow-up when a regular omoplata is almost finished but the opponent is escaping

ibjjf.note: Shoulder lock, not on the prohibited table

summary: A Marcelo Garcia omoplata follow-up used when the opponent is slipping out of the standard omoplata.
notes: Only a Grapplearts tag page (video tutorial) was located; written mechanics are not described in text, so the exact leg/grip configuration is unverified.

name: Shoulder lock from the crucifix (reverse omoplata / leg kimura)

primary_target.mechanism: Forced internal rotation with the arm driven behind the back by the legs: the arm captured between the thighs is bent, and the attacker rotates the hips away from the trapped arm (opposite direction to a standard omoplata), while wrist control stops the opponent spinning out
primary_target.plain: The arm trapped between your thighs is bent and your legs drive it up their back as you turn your hips away from it (the opposite way to an omoplata), twisting the shoulder joint inward; holding the wrist stops them rolling out. This stretches the back of the shoulder joint and the rotator cuff.

positions.note: Force the 'arm down' position, then kimura-style lock applied with the legs
Crucifix is usually entered from turtle/arm drag

ibjjf.note: Shoulder lock, not on the prohibited table

summary: With the arm isolated between your legs in the crucifix, rotate the hips to bend the arm up the back like a leg-driven kimura.

sources.locator: Biernacki 'arm down' kimura-style armlock with the legs

name: Hammerlock / chicken wing

primary_target.mechanism: Forced internal rotation and extension: the arm is bent behind the opponent's back and the hand is driven up toward the neck/scapula, placing pressure on the shoulder
primary_target.plain: Their arm is bent behind their back and the hand is pushed up toward the neck or shoulder blade, twisting the shoulder joint inward and backward and stretching the back of the shoulder joint and the rotator cuff.

secondary_targets.mechanism: Elbow is flexed and used as the lever; a 'twisting hammerlock' adds elbow torque
secondary_targets.plain: The bent elbow is the lever; a 'twisting hammerlock' adds a twist on the elbow too.

positions.note: Arm levered behind the back from the top of turtle
Classic standing control/pin from behind
Arm driven up the back

ibjjf.note: Not on the IBJJF prohibited table; in BJJ it usually appears as a kimura/'chicken wing' finish rather than a stand-alone technique

summary: Arm bent behind the back and hand pushed up toward the neck; the oldest documented armlock, now mostly a wrestling/control idea or kimura variant.
notes: No BJJ textbook locator; the 1928 NCAA rulebook banned the twisting hammerlock in wrestling, but it is not listed by the IBJJF.

name: Mir lock

primary_target.mechanism: Forced internal rotation with the elbow clamped: a figure-four grip on the wrist with the opponent's elbow pinned tightly to the attacker's chest/hip, then the wrist is rotated toward the opponent's back ('paintbrush') so all torque goes to the shoulder
primary_target.plain: With a figure-four grip on the wrist and their elbow pinned tight to your chest or hip, you rotate the wrist toward their back (the 'paintbrush') so all of the twist goes into the shoulder, twisting the shoulder joint inward and stretching the back of the shoulder joint and the rotator cuff.

secondary_targets.mechanism: Elbow is trapped and compressed against the chest; some descriptions say it attacks elbow and shoulder together
secondary_targets.plain: The elbow is trapped and squeezed against your chest; some descriptions say this attacks the elbow and shoulder at the same time.

positions.note: Named for Frank Mir's finish of Pete Williams (UFC 36, 2002); overhook the arm, sit up and lock the figure-four as the opponent pulls away
Digitsu describes it from kesa-gatame / combat base with hip pressure

ibjjf.note: A shoulder lock, not on the prohibited table (it is NOT a wrist lock, so no blue-belt restriction)

summary: A tight kimura/keylock hybrid with the elbow trapped against your body and the wrist rotated toward the opponent's back.
notes: Sources conflict: some call it a kimura variant, some an americana variant with elbow/shoulder together. The task brief grouped it with supination wrist locks; the located sources describe a shoulder lock. Origin (Mir vs Williams UFC 36) not verified in the sources retrieved.

name: Bicep slicer

structures: biceps brachii and brachialis muscle bellies
primary_target.mechanism: Compression: a bony fulcrum (shin, forearm/radius, or wrist) is wedged deep into the antecubital fossa and the forearm is forcibly flexed over it, crushing the biceps/brachialis and distal biceps tendon against the humerus
primary_target.plain: A hard edge - your shin, forearm bone or wrist - is jammed deep into the bend of their elbow and their forearm is folded over it, crushing the biceps, the muscle under it and the biceps tendon against the upper-arm bone.

secondary_targets.mechanism: The fulcrum inside the bent elbow distracts/separates the joint (why judo treats it as an armlock)
secondary_targets.plain: The wedge in the bend of the elbow levers the joint apart, which is why judo counts it as an armlock.

positions.note: Thread the arm inside the elbow, control the wrist, open the guard and fold the arm over your forearm
Shin across the elbow crease provides the fulcrum
Shin-in-elbow slicers appear in 10th Planet material
After a defended mounted armbar: leg over the forearm, lock a triangle and squeeze
From a defended kimura, go deeper into the figure-four with the forearm as the blade
Pin the near arm with the inside leg and drive the hips

ibjjf.note: IBJJF Rules Book v6.1 p. 29 table row 12: prohibited for all kids/juvenile divisions and for adult white, blue and purple belts; permitted for adult brown and black belts (gi and no-gi)

summary: Fold the opponent's arm over your shin or forearm wedged in the crook of the elbow and squeeze the biceps against the bone.
notes: Legality verified against the rendered IBJJF table (2026-10-11). Rubber guard position cited to Bravo without a page locator.

name: Wrist lock - flexion (gooseneck)

primary_target.mechanism: Forced palmar flexion of the wrist past its end range: the hand is pushed toward the inner forearm while the forearm/elbow is immobilised (elbow and shoulder must be controlled so the opponent cannot roll the arm out)
primary_target.plain: Their hand is bent toward the inside of the forearm past its limit while you pin the elbow and shoulder so they cannot roll the arm out. This stretches the ligaments and tendons on the back of the wrist.

positions.note: Against a hand posted on the chest or a collar/lapel grip: cup the triceps, fold the hand with your chest/hands and drive the hips forward
Fold the wrist of a hand pushing on the chest/hip
From a kimura grip: hands control the wrist, biceps the elbow, ribs the shoulder (Kesting)
'Sitting on the shoulder' after an omoplata sweep: belly and hand control the wrist, calf/hamstring clamp the shoulder
Against a gi collar grip the trapped wrist is folded (gi only); rarely finishes standing

ibjjf.note: IBJJF Rules Book v6.1 p. 29 table row 10 'Wrist lock': prohibited for 4-12, 13-15, 16-17 (all ranks) and all white-belt divisions; permitted for adult blue belt and above (gi and no-gi)

summary: Bend the hand toward the inside of the forearm while the elbow and shoulder are pinned - the 'gooseneck'.
notes: Legality verified against the rendered IBJJF table (2026-10-11); earlier blog claims of purple/brown thresholds are wrong for the current rules. A wristlock 'from spider guard' was requested but no source describing it was found, so it is omitted.

name: Wrist lock - hyperextension

primary_target.mechanism: Forced dorsiflexion/hyperextension: the knuckles are driven back toward the forearm, usually by pinning the palm flat and driving weight through the straight arm, or by bending the hand back against a trapped forearm
primary_target.plain: Their knuckles are driven back toward the forearm, bending the wrist back past its limit - usually by pinning the palm flat and driving weight through their straight arm. This stretches the ligaments and tendons on the palm side of the wrist.

secondary_targets.mechanism: Often combined with finger extension - illegal if fingers are bent backwards (IBJJF row 24)
secondary_targets.plain: Often combined with bending the fingers back - illegal under IBJJF rules if the fingers are bent backwards.

positions.note: Against a stiff arm posted on the chest: pin the hand flat to your chest and sit up/drive the hips
Pin a framing hand flat to your shoulder/chest and press
Counter when the opponent grabs your wrist: grab four fingers/hand and turn the hand back (Evolve)

ibjjf.note: Wrist lock row 10: legal from adult blue belt. Bending the fingers backwards (row 24) is prohibited at every level, so the hand must be controlled as a whole

summary: Pin the palm and drive the knuckles back toward the forearm; weak on its own, strong against a stiff-arm frame.

name: Wrist lock - rotational (supination / pronation)

primary_target.mechanism: Forced supination or pronation beyond end range: the wrist itself does not rotate, so the twist is transmitted to the distal and proximal radioulnar joints and, with the elbow straightened, to the shoulder; usually combined with flexion (kote-gaeshi) or pronation with the elbow bent (nikyo/sankyo)
primary_target.plain: The hand is twisted palm-up or palm-down past its limit. The wrist itself does not twist, so the strain goes into the joints between the two forearm bones (at the wrist and near the elbow) and the cartilage on the little-finger side of the wrist; with the elbow straight it carries on into the shoulder.

secondary_targets.mechanism: Torsion of the forearm bones
secondary_targets.plain: The two forearm bones are twisted against each other.

secondary_targets.mechanism: With a straight elbow the rotation ends at the shoulder
secondary_targets.plain: With a straight elbow the twist ends at the shoulder.

positions.note: Sankyo-style palm-down twisting wristlock from rear mount (Kesting)
Palm-up twist on a hand that grips your collar/lapel (gi) or posts on the chest
From the kimura grip, rotate the hand rather than the shoulder
Kote-gaeshi style takedown-wristlock; low percentage in competition because elbow/shoulder are free

ibjjf.note: Wrist lock row 10: legal from adult blue belt; prohibited for all juvenile and white-belt divisions

summary: Twist the hand fully palm-up or palm-down while the elbow is pinned so the forearm joints, not the wrist, take the torque.

sources.locator: Rotational, supinating and pronating wristlock sections
sankyo from rear mount; kimura-grip finish

notes: The brief's 'supination/Mir lock' label does not match located sources: the Mir lock is documented as a shoulder lock (see mir_lock).

name: Finger lock / small-joint manipulation

primary_target.mechanism: Hyperextension (or lateral deviation) of one or more fingers against the volar plate and collateral ligaments
primary_target.plain: One or more fingers are bent backwards (or sideways) past their limit, stretching the ligaments on the palm side and edges of the finger joints.

positions.note: Any grip-fighting situation; shown here only so the hand region surfaces the rule

ibjjf.note: IBJJF Rules Book v6.1 p. 29 table row 24 'Bending fingers backwards' is prohibited in every division, gi and no-gi. Grabbing fewer than four fingers to break a grip is also restricted (item 6.2.2 H concerns fingers inside the sleeve/pant opening)

summary: Bending fingers back is banned at all belts under IBJJF rules; wrist locks on the whole hand are legal from blue belt.

sources.locator: note on combining hyperextending wristlocks with fingerlocks

notes: Included as a legality marker rather than a taught technique.

name: Two-on-one (Russian tie)

primary_target.mechanism: Both of the attacker's hands control one arm: far hand on the wrist, near hand under the armpit or on the triceps/elbow, body behind the arm with the shoulder above the opponent's, breaking posture and removing the arm from the fight
primary_target.plain: Both your hands control one of their arms - one on the wrist, one under the armpit or on the back of the upper arm - with your body behind the arm and your shoulder above theirs. Nothing is hurt: it breaks their posture and takes that arm out of the fight.

secondary_targets.mechanism: Wrist grip pins the hand to the attacker's hip
secondary_targets.plain: Your grip pins their hand to your hip.

positions.note: Wrestling tie leading to sumi-gaeshi, arm drag, blast double, drop ouchi, back take or ude-garami
Marcelo Garcia's seated 2-on-1 to arm drag/back take or omoplata
Seated guard 2-on-1 grip

summary: Two hands on one arm from the outside: a wrestling tie that kills the opponent's posture and leads to arm drags, back takes and shoulder locks.
notes: Garcia 2011 and Mastering Jujitsu page numbers not verified.

name: Wrist control

primary_target.mechanism: Gripping the wrist (or sleeve cuff) to deny posts, grips and frames; the hand is pinned to the mat or the attacker's body so the elbow and shoulder can be attacked
primary_target.plain: Holding the wrist (or sleeve cuff) stops them posting, gripping or framing, and pins the hand to the mat or your body so you can attack the elbow and shoulder.

positions.note: Grip fighting: control the wrist to set up arm drags, snap-downs and 2-on-1s
Wrist + collar tie to set up the armbar and kimura
Pin the near wrist to the mat/hip to open americana/kimura
Pin a wrist to the mat for the americana or to isolate for the armbar
Control the defending hand/wrist to open the choke

ibjjf.note: Gripping inside the sleeve/pant cuff with the fingers is a penalty (item 6.2.2 H)

summary: The most basic arm control: hold the wrist to remove the hand from play and expose the elbow and shoulder.

name: Arm drag

primary_target.mechanism: Same-side wrist grip plus a cup on the triceps; the arm is pulled across the attacker's body so the opponent's back is exposed, usually leading to a rear clinch or back take
primary_target.plain: You grip their wrist on the same side and cup the back of the upper arm, then pull the arm across your body so their back is exposed. It is a control, not a submission - it leads to a back take.

positions.note: Grip the wrist, cup the triceps, step offline and swing the arm past you to the rear clinch
Marcelo Garcia's signature: cup the triceps, hook outside, pull forward and shift the hips to take the back (or sweep)
Seated guard arm drag
Arm drag entry to the crucifix

summary: Pull the arm across your body by the wrist and triceps to get behind the opponent.

name: Gift wrap

structures: humerus / shoulder (arm folded across the face)
primary_target.mechanism: One of the opponent's arms is folded across their own face/neck and pinned: in no-gi the attacker grips the wrist deep behind the head from the opposite side; in gi the opponent's own lapel is fed over the arm; chest pressure keeps them flat
primary_target.plain: One of their arms is folded across their own face and neck and pinned there - you hold the wrist from behind the head, or in the gi their own lapel is fed over the arm - while your chest keeps them flat.

secondary_targets.mechanism: The trapped forearm lies across the face, limiting head movement
secondary_targets.plain: Their own forearm lies across their face, so they cannot move the head much.

structures: opponent's own arm wrapped across the neck
secondary_targets.mechanism: The opponent's arm is pulled across their own throat and pinned there with a 2-on-1 / kimura-style grip from behind the head; the trapped arm immobilises the head and shoulders and exposes the back
secondary_targets.plain: Their arm is pulled across their own throat and held from behind the head, which pins the head and shoulders and opens up their back.

secondary_targets.mechanism: Arm wrapped across the body
secondary_targets.plain: The arm is wrapped across their body, turning the shoulder inward.

secondary_targets.mechanism: Wrist gripped behind the neck
secondary_targets.plain: You hold their wrist behind their neck.

positions.note: From mount/technical mount; leads to back take, armbar or chokes
Feed the near arm across the face and pin it
Standard follow-up from the gift wrap
Seen in top half guard and 3/4 mount

ibjjf.note: Control only; pressing the forearm into the face is legal but hands blocking nose/mouth airflow is a severe foul (6.2.3 J)

summary: Fold the opponent's arm across their own face and hold the wrist from the other side; a Rickson-era control leading to the back, crucifix or armbar.
notes: Attribution to Rickson Gracie is from secondary blogs, not verified in a textbook. Merged with the torso-control entry from the neck/torso research set.

name: Overhook / whizzer

primary_target.mechanism: The attacker's arm goes over the opponent's arm and encircles it (or the upper body), lifting the armpit and shoulder; from the guard it clamps the arm to the attacker's ribs to deny posture and set up omoplata, kimura, reverse armbar or triangle
primary_target.plain: Your arm goes over their arm and wraps it (or their upper body), lifting their armpit and shoulder; from guard it clamps their arm to your ribs so they cannot posture up, setting up the omoplata, kimura, reverse armbar or triangle.

positions.note: Whizzer vs underhook/single-leg attempts
Overhook guard: kimura/omoplata/reverse armbar/triangle set-ups
Whizzer to counter the bottom player's underhook
Overhook + wrist control sweeps

summary: Arm over the opponent's arm, lifting the shoulder; the standard answer to an underhook and a rich attacking grip from guard.

sources.locator: overhook clamp for the reverse armbar

name: Underhook

primary_target.mechanism: The attacker's arm goes under the opponent's arm and the hand grips the back/shoulder blade, lifting the shoulder and controlling the torso; it elevates the opponent's arm away from their body and gives access to the back and to takedowns
primary_target.plain: Your arm goes under their arm and your hand grips their back or shoulder blade, lifting the shoulder and lifting their arm away from their body so you control the upper body and can get to the back or a takedown.

secondary_targets.mechanism: Attacker's arm passes under the opponent's arm and controls the back or shoulder, lifting the opponent's elbow and taking control of the upper torso to direct their weight
secondary_targets.plain: Your arm under theirs controls their back or shoulder, lifting their elbow so you can steer their upper body and weight.

positions.note: Clinch control for takedowns and back takes; too deep an underhook concedes a whizzer
Underhook from half guard for the dogfight/back take
Cross-face + underhook flattens the bottom player
Far-side underhook pins the far arm/shoulder
Underhook + butterfly hook sweep
The bottom player's underhook is the key to half-guard sweeps; the top player's underhook plus cross-face is the key to passing
Underhook to stand up / wrestle up

summary: Arm under the opponent's arm with the hand on their back - the foundational clinch and half-guard control.

sources.locator: relation of overhooks to underhooks; cites Evolve 'Understanding Underhooks And Overhooks'

notes: Merged with the torso-control entry from the neck/torso research set.

name: Kimura grip as a control position

primary_target.mechanism: The figure-four kimura grip is held as a 'giant handle': it immobilises the arm, threatens the shoulder lock, and is used to sweep, pass, take the back, or transition between kimura positions (side control, north-south, near-side, T-kimura, back)
primary_target.plain: The figure-four kimura grip is held as a big handle: it locks up the arm, keeps the shoulder lock threatened and lets you sweep, pass, take the back or move between kimura positions.

secondary_targets.mechanism: Latent kimura threat
secondary_targets.plain: The kimura on the shoulder is always one move away.

positions.note: Kimura grip to sweep/back take; 'kimura trap' systems (Avellan)
Kimura sweep when the lock is defended
Kimura-based guard passing and pinning
Topside kimura control vs turtle to roll the opponent
Kimura control from the back
Kimura grip on a single-leg attempt

summary: Treat the kimura grip as a position, not just a finish: it controls the arm and moves the opponent between side, north-south, back and sweeps.

name: Side control arm isolation (cross-face + far-arm trap)

structures: near arm (trapped against the attacker's hip)
primary_target.mechanism: The cross-face arm turns the head away while the other arm underhooks the far arm, or the far arm is trapped under the attacker's armpit; the near arm is pinned between the attacker's hip and the opponent's body, isolating both arms for americana, kimura and armbar
primary_target.plain: Your cross-face turns their head away while your other arm underhooks or traps their far arm under your armpit; their near arm is pinned between your hip and their body, so both arms are isolated for the americana, kimura or armbar.

secondary_targets.mechanism: Cross-face turns the head to kill the bridge
secondary_targets.plain: The cross-face turns their head away so they cannot bridge.

positions.note: Standard side control pin; first stage of the far-arm kimura/armbar
Arms trapped under the armpits
Far arm pinned by the hand on the collar/shoulder

ibjjf.note: Legal; the forearm may press the face but the hands must not block nose/mouth airflow (6.2.3 J)

summary: Before any top-side arm attack the far arm is isolated under the armpit or with an underhook while the cross-face controls the head.
notes: Ribeiro page numbers not verified.

name: S-mount arm isolation

primary_target.mechanism: From high mount the attacker's legs form an 'S': one knee behind the head, the other shin across the chest, so the opponent's arm is trapped against the thigh and the elbow cannot retreat; the near knee blocks the head, separating the arm from the body for the armbar, baratoplata or monoplata
primary_target.plain: From high mount your legs make an 'S' - one knee behind their head, the other shin across their chest - so their arm is trapped against your thigh and the elbow cannot pull back, separating the arm from their body for the armbar, baratoplata or monoplata.

secondary_targets.mechanism: Shin across the chest pins the torso
secondary_targets.plain: Your shin across their chest pins their upper body.

positions.note: Primary position
Transition from high mount when the opponent pushes the chest/hips
Closely related arm trap

ibjjf.note: Mount points are not awarded if the leg trapping the arm extends beyond the opponent's shoulder line (IBJJF 3.4 note); the control itself is legal

summary: The asymmetrical high mount that pins one arm against your thigh and blocks the head with your knee - the launch pad for mounted armbars.

sources.locator: mount scoring note (leg trapping the arm not beyond the shoulder)

name: Spider guard (foot-on-biceps control)

primary_target.mechanism: Four-finger or hook grips on both sleeves with the feet pressing the biceps (aim for the crook of the arm) create push-pull tension that controls posture, base and distance and pre-extends the arms for armbar, triangle and omoplata
primary_target.plain: You grip both sleeves and press your feet into their biceps (aim for the bend of the arm); the push-pull controls their posture, base and distance and keeps their arms straight, setting up the armbar, triangle and omoplata.

secondary_targets.mechanism: Sleeve grip near the wrist
secondary_targets.plain: Your sleeve grip sits near the wrist.

positions.note: Primary position (gi)
Entered from seated/open guard sleeve grips
One foot on the biceps, the other leg lassoed

ibjjf.note: Requires the gi sleeve

summary: Sleeve grips plus feet on the biceps: the gi open guard that keeps the arms straight and the opponent's posture broken.

name: Lasso guard (lasso hook)

primary_target.mechanism: With a sleeve grip, the leg spirals outside and around the opponent's arm so the shin lies across the biceps and the foot hooks into the armpit or back; the trapped arm cannot post or grip and the shoulder is pulled down, breaking posture
primary_target.plain: With a sleeve grip, your leg wraps around the outside of their arm so your shin lies across the biceps and your foot hooks into the armpit or back; the trapped arm cannot post or grip and their shoulder is pulled down, breaking posture.

secondary_targets.mechanism: Same-side sleeve grip is pulled constantly
secondary_targets.plain: You keep pulling on the same-side sleeve.

positions.note: Primary position; attacks: omoplata, triangle, sweeps, bicep slicer, back take
Combined spider-lasso
Lasso + DLR hook

ibjjf.note: Gi only (sleeve-dependent). Bicep slicer finishes from the lasso remain brown-belt-only

summary: A leg wrapped around the arm with the shin on the biceps: harder to strip than spider guard and a direct door to the omoplata.

name: Crucifix (arm trapped between the legs)

structures: upper arm / elbow (clamped between the attacker's thighs)
far arm (controlled by the attacker's arms/seatbelt)
primary_target.mechanism: One of the opponent's arms is isolated between the attacker's thighs (often triangled) while the other is controlled with the hands, spreading the arms like a cross; the trapped arm can be armbarred, keylocked or rotated with the legs, and the free hands attack the neck
primary_target.plain: One of their arms is trapped between your thighs (often with your legs locked) and the other is held by your hands, spreading their arms out like a cross; the trapped arm can be armbarred, keylocked or twisted with your legs, and your free hands can attack the neck.

secondary_targets.mechanism: Chokes become available with both of the opponent's arms occupied
secondary_targets.plain: With both their arms tied up, chokes on the neck - on the arteries or the windpipe - are open.

positions.note: Primary position
Entered from side-ride on turtle or from an arm drag; lock the thighs on the arm and lift with the outside leg

ibjjf.note: Control is legal; bicep-slicer finishes from here are brown-belt-only

summary: Both of the opponent's arms are tied up - one by your legs, one by your arms - so that nothing can defend the chokes and leg-armlocks that follow.
